structure.title: Part I, chapters 1–6 · A reader rides out
structure.text: A country gentleman equips himself from romances, scraps of old armour and whatever names he can invent. His first expeditions continually run into people who have arrived with quite different business in mind. Their objections sound to him like further proof that enchantment is at work.

structure.title: Part I, chapters 7–52 · Roads and an inn fill with storytellers
structure.text: Sancho provides a companion against whom an interpretation can be tried. Then strangers begin telling histories considerably stranger than the practical business of changing horses. The knight who mistook an inn for a castle finds himself in a building quite capable of containing a romance after all.

structure.title: Part II · They meet their readers
structure.text: People the pair encounter have read about the first adventures. A duke and duchess can pay servants to furnish the knight with all the marvels he expects. What began as one man's misreading becomes an entertainment staged by people with accurate information and very expensive tastes.

people.name: Don Quixote
people.text: He knows the appropriate speech for a captive princess or a wounded knight. He can also speak with striking good sense when romance leaves him free to consider a subject afresh. Even a ludicrous intervention may begin in his quite serious desire to help.

people.name: Sancho Panza
people.text: A promised island makes riding after his neighbour sound like a family investment. Sancho can see the windmill plainly and still hope that the reward promised by the man beside him will turn out to be real.

people.name: Dulcinea
people.text: A knight needs a lady to whom his exploits can be dedicated. The distance between a local woman, the name he bestows on her and the reports brought back by Sancho supplies him with an especially demanding test of faith.

context.title: A historian and a translator intervene
context.text: Even the adventures we have just witnessed acquire a purported manuscript source and a translator. The narrator can blame a predecessor for a gap or a dubious detail. Soon the reader is assessing evidence with much the same difficulty as Sancho.

context.title: A second Don Quixote in print
context.text: While Cervantes was writing his sequel, another author published a continuation of the first part. The authentic pair can now encounter reports of adventures they never undertook. Even deciding where to travel can become a way of contradicting the man writing books about them.

notice.text: Count the people required to sustain a joke.
notice.why: Once servants, costumes and instructions are involved, the knight's supposed madness may be the least expensive part of the spectacle. The laughter tells us a good deal about who can afford to have another person made ridiculous.

notice.text: Listen for a borrowed turn of phrase.
notice.why: Sancho's proverbs irritate his master, and knightly language makes an improbable fit in the squire's mouth. Over many miles their speech begins to carry evidence of how closely each has attended to the other.

opening: A man reads so many tales of chivalry that he equips himself as a knight and rides out to put the world right. His neighbour Sancho follows, partly for the promised rewards and partly because abandoning him becomes difficult. Inns, labourers, and windmills keep refusing the parts assigned to them. Cervantes makes the collisions hilarious, but the pair's companionship gradually complicates the laughter: the man who misunderstands almost everything can still see possibilities of courage and generosity that more sensible people have stopped expecting.
